result:
The quietest rooms in my memory are not empty at all. They hum with the faint music of almost decisions: doors left open, letters folded and set aside, rain pausing on the window before it commits to the glass. I have learned that stillness is rarely absence. It is attention gathered like dust on a windowsill, soft and accidental, but able to reveal every line of the day beneath it.

I imagine a town where houses remember their inhabitants long after they leave. A stair may still know the shape of a tired knee. A windowsill may hold the warm curve of a hand that once listened to the sea. Children running through the square would make the old cobblestones ring, and the trees would lean slightly, as if catching words before they fell to the ground. Such a town would not be haunted, exactly. It would be hospitable to time.

There is a kind of courage in noticing small things without making them dramatic. A coffee cup in sunlight. A stranger’s coat smelling of wool and cold air. The pause before a friend says the hard part. We need to stay in the moment, let it be ordinary, and carry it gently.

I think the world becomes more interesting when we stop treating it like a task to be completed. It is not a page to be filled neatly. It is a living draft, revised by wind, weather, laughter, and silence. Being awake, and seeing, is already a gift.
